join-condition.def: The test after ON that says which rows belong together, like c.id = o.customer_id.

inner-join.def: Keeps only rows that have a match on both sides. Anything without a partner, on either side, is dropped. Plain JOIN means inner join.

left-join.def: Keeps every row of the left table. Where there's no match on the right, the right side's columns are NULL.

anti-join.def: Finds rows with no match in another table, for example with a left join and a test for NULL on the right side.

right-join.def: The mirror of a left join: keeps every row of the right table. Usually written as a left join with the tables swapped.

full-outer-join.def: Keeps every row from both tables, matched where possible, with NULLs where a side has no partner.

fan-out.def: A join that matches several rows per row, so the first table's rows repeat. Totals from that side get counted more than once.

cross-join.def: Every row of one table paired with every row of the other: rows times rows. What you get when a join has no condition.

lines.hook.1: Maya's orders don't store her name. They store her customer ID, a key that points into the customers table.
lines.hook.2: Remember following those pointers by hand? In SQL, that's one clause: JOIN.
lines.hook.3: But every kind of join quietly drops some rows, or repeats them. Knowing which is what interviewers check.
lines.inner.1: Customers on the left, orders on the right. Each order carries a customer ID.

inner.2.caption: JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id matches each order to the customer it points at.
inner.2.voice: Join customers, on the customer's ID equals the order's customer ID. That matches each order to the customer it points at.

lines.inner.3: The part after ON is the <k id="join-condition">join condition</k>. It says which rows belong together.
lines.inner.4: Some rows have no partner. Lena and Theo never ordered, and two walk-in orders have no customer at all.
lines.inner.ask: Sixteen orders go in. How many rows come out?
lines.inner.sixteen: Close, but the two walk-ins have nobody to match. Fourteen.
lines.inner.fourteen: Fourteen. You were watching the walk-ins.
lines.inner.ten: More than that. Fourteen orders have a customer, so fourteen rows come back.
lines.inner.5: An <k id="inner-join">inner join</k> keeps only matched pairs. Anything without a partner, on either side, is dropped.
lines.inner.6: Plain JOIN means inner join. It's the default.
lines.left.1: Now the bakery wants every customer, with their orders if they have any.
lines.left.2: Swap JOIN for LEFT JOIN. Every row from the left table stays.
lines.left.3: Lena and Theo stay too. Where an order should be, the columns are filled with NULL.
lines.left.4: That's a <k id="left-join">left join</k>: all of the left table, plus its matches from the right, or NULLs.
lines.never.1: The bakery wants to send a welcome offer to customers who've never ordered.
lines.never.2: Here's the trick. After a left join, those customers are the rows where the order side is NULL.
lines.never.ask: Finish the WHERE clause, then run it.

never.hint.caption: Keep the rows where o.id IS NULL.
never.hint.voice: Keep the rows where the order's ID is null.

lines.never.error: The database couldn't run that. The message under the editor says why.
lines.never.extra: Too many rows. Keep only the customers whose order side is NULL.
lines.never.missing: Someone's missing. Test the order's ID with IS NULL, not with equals.
lines.never.done: Lena and Theo. Finding rows with no match is called an <k id="anti-join">anti-join</k>.
lines.trap.1: Next request: every customer, with their paid orders. Customers with none should still show up.
lines.trap.2: A first try: a left join, then keep the paid orders in WHERE.
lines.trap.ask: Will Lena still be in the result?

trap.3.caption: Lena, Theo and Raj are gone. WHERE runs after the join, and a NULL status isn't 'paid'.
trap.3.voice: Lena, Theo and Raj are gone. WHERE runs after the join, and a null status isn't paid, so their rows fail.

lines.trap.4: A filter on the right-hand table in WHERE quietly turns a left join back into an inner join.
lines.trap.5: Move the test into ON. Now it only decides which orders match, and every customer stays.
lines.trap.6: Rule of thumb: in a left join, filters on the right-hand table belong in ON.
lines.full.1: A <k id="right-join">right join</k> is the mirror image: it keeps every row of the right table. Most teams swap the tables and write LEFT.
lines.full.2: A <k id="full-outer-join">full outer join</k> keeps both sides whole: customers with no orders, and orders with no customer.
lines.full.3: Eighteen rows. It's handy for reconciling two lists, to see what's missing on each side.
lines.fanout.1: Joins can also add rows. Each order has one or more items.
lines.fanout.2: Join orders to their items, and sixteen orders become twenty-two rows. Order one appears twice, once per item.
lines.fanout.3: That's <k id="fan-out">fan-out</k>. Add up anything from the orders side now, and some orders count twice.
lines.fanout.4: Forget the join condition entirely, and every customer pairs with every order. Ten times sixteen: a hundred and sixty rows.
lines.fanout.5: That's a <k id="cross-join">cross join</k>. Occasionally useful, usually a bug.
lines.fanout.6: Before trusting a joined total, ask: how many rows per order does this join make?
lines.walk.1: Last one. List every order's ID with the customer's name, and keep the walk-in orders.
lines.walk.ask: Write the join. Start from the orders.

walk.hint.caption: Start FROM orders, then LEFT JOIN customers.
walk.hint.voice: Start from orders, then left join customers.

lines.walk.error: The database couldn't run that. Read the message, then try again.
lines.walk.extra: Too many rows. Check the ON condition.
lines.walk.missing: Some orders are missing. The walk-ins need a left join that starts from orders.
lines.walk.columns: Just the order's ID and the customer's name.
lines.walk.done: Sixteen orders, two with no name. Which table comes first decides what a left join keeps.

quiz.q1.caption: customers has 10 rows, orders has 16, and 2 orders have no customer. How many rows does an inner join on the customer ID return?
quiz.q1.voice: Customers has ten rows. Orders has sixteen, and two have no customer. How many rows does an inner join on the customer ID return?
quiz.q1.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q1-why: Each order with a customer matches exactly one row, so fourteen. The walk-ins, and customers who never ordered, are dropped.

quiz.q2.caption: Which query finds customers who have never ordered?
quiz.q2.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q2-why: A left join keeps every customer. Those with no order have NULL on the order side, so test for that.

quiz.q3.caption: LEFT JOIN orders o ON … WHERE o.status = 'paid'. What happens to customers with no paid orders?
quiz.q3.voice: A left join to orders, then where the status is paid. What happens to customers with no paid orders?
quiz.q3.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q3-why: WHERE runs after the join, and NULL isn't paid, so those rows fail. Put the condition in ON.

quiz.q4.caption: A report's revenue doubled right after someone added a join. What's the likely cause?
quiz.q4.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q4-why: The new join matches several rows per order, so each order is repeated, and added up, more than once.

quiz.retry.caption: {right} / 4. Worth another pass.
quiz.retry.voice: Not quite there. Replay a chapter or two, then try again.

lines.keywords.1: Before we wrap up, here are the words worth keeping.
lines.keywords.ask: Flip each card. Star the ones you want to practise later.
lines.keywords.hint: Tap a card to flip it. Press Done when you're ready.
lines.keywords.done: Starred words go to your flashcards. A few minutes a day keeps them fresh.
lines.finish.1: That's the lesson. Inner joins keep only matches. Outer joins keep a side whole, with NULLs. And joins can multiply rows.
lines.finish.2: Next up: turning rows into numbers, with GROUP BY.
